# A Regression Model for Clustered Gaussian Data

Linear mixed-effects models extend linear regression by adding latent effects
shared by observations in the same group. They are useful for repeated measures,
longitudinal data, multi-site experiments, blocked designs, pedigrees, and nested
sampling structures. Their central task is not merely to “correct” standard
errors. They jointly describe the conditional mean and the covariance created by
the sampling hierarchy.

For all observations stacked into a vector,

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf Z\mathbf b+\boldsymbol\varepsilon,
\qquad
\mathbf b\sim N(\mathbf0,\mathbf G),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim N(\mathbf0,\mathbf R).
}
$$

$\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$ is the fixed-effect mean structure,
$\mathbf Z\mathbf b$ contains random effects, and $\mathbf R$ describes residual
variation. The usual model assumes $\mathbf b$ and
$\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ are independent. Integrating out $\mathbf b$ gives the
marginal model

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf y\sim N(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf V),
\qquad
\mathbf V=\mathbf Z\mathbf G\mathbf Z^\mathsf{T}+\mathbf R.
}
$$

This identity connects hierarchical interpretation to generalized least
squares. Random effects are one structured way to build $\mathbf V$; they are
not the only possible covariance model.

# Start with the Scientific Target and Experimental Unit

Before writing a formula, define the target population, independent sampling
unit, outcome, predictor levels, and desired generalization.

| Goal | Example estimand | Relevant level |
|---|---|---|
| Population mean comparison | mean treatment contrast $\mathbf c^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\beta$ | target population of biological units |
| Heterogeneity | donor-level variance component in $\mathbf G$ | variation among donors |
| Existing-unit prediction | conditional mean given estimated $\mathbf b_i$ | a sampled donor or site |
| New-unit prediction | outcome integrated over a new $\mathbf b_{\mathrm{new}}$ | a future donor or site |

The **estimand** is the population quantity in the scientific question. ML or
REML fitting supplies an **estimator**, a random function of the data. Its
observed coefficient or variance component is an **estimate**. A conditional
prediction for a sampled donor is not the same target as a population-average
fixed effect or a prediction for a new donor.

Fixed and random are properties of the model and inferential target, not innate
properties of variables. A treatment is often represented by fixed coefficients
because its specific contrast is the target. A donor effect may be random when
donors are viewed as sampled from a population and their distribution is used
for pooling. The number of levels alone does not decide the choice.

# Conditional and Marginal Interpretation

Conditional on $\mathbf b$, the mean is

$$
E(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf b)=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+
\mathbf Z\mathbf b.
$$

Marginal over the random effects,

$$
E(\mathbf y)=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta.
$$

For an identity-link Gaussian model, the fixed-effect coefficient has the same
linear scale in both expressions, although predictions differ according to
whether random effects are included. This convenient equality generally fails
after a nonlinear link, which is one reason generalized linear mixed-model
coefficients require special care.

Consider a donor random-intercept model,

$$
Y_{ij}=\beta_0+\beta_1T_{ij}+b_i+\varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad b_i\sim N(0,\tau^2).
$$

$\beta_1$ is a conditional mean contrast at the modeled covariate values. A
causal interpretation additionally needs treatment assignment, consistency,
positivity, and control of confounding. The random effect accounts for modeled
dependence; it does not by itself control unmeasured time-varying confounding.

# Likelihood and Generalized Least Squares

For known covariance parameters in $\mathbf V$, maximizing the Gaussian
likelihood over $\boldsymbol\beta$ gives

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{GLS}}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf y,
$$

with model-based covariance

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X)
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}.
$$

In practice, covariance parameters
$\boldsymbol\theta$ inside $\mathbf G$ and $\mathbf R$ are unknown. The
log-likelihood, apart from a constant, is

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)
=-\frac12\left[
\log|\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}|
+(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^\mathsf{T}
\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
\right].
$$

Maximum likelihood estimates fixed effects and covariance parameters jointly.
Restricted maximum likelihood (REML) instead maximizes a likelihood for error
contrasts that remove the fixed-effect degrees of freedom. One form of the REML
criterion adds

$$
\log|\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf X|
$$

to the bracketed ML expression. REML often reduces small-sample bias in variance
components, but it is not universally unbiased and does not rescue a
misspecified covariance or mean model.

# ML, REML, and Model Comparison

The estimation method must match the comparison.

- Use ML, not REML, to compare nested models with different fixed-effect columns
  by a likelihood-ratio statistic, because REML criteria are based on different
  error-contrast spaces.
- REML criteria can compare covariance structures when the fixed-effect design
  is identical and regularity conditions are appropriate.
- Refit the selected fixed-effect structure with REML when REML variance estimates
  and associated summaries are the reporting target.
- Information criteria are comparable only when based on the same response data,
  likelihood convention, and compatible estimation target.

Likelihood-ratio reference distributions can fail for testing a variance
component equal to zero because the null lies on a boundary. Small numbers of
groups also make large-sample chi-squared and normal approximations unreliable.
Parametric bootstrap, restricted-likelihood methods with justified reference
distributions, or carefully calibrated small-sample procedures may be preferable.

# Fixed-effect Inference

For a prespecified contrast $\psi=\mathbf c^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\beta$, the
estimate is $\widehat\psi=\mathbf c^\mathsf{T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ with
plug-in standard error

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\psi)
=\sqrt{
\mathbf c^\mathsf{T}
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
\mathbf c}.
$$

Wald intervals and tests often use a normal or approximate $t$ reference
distribution. The denominator degrees of freedom are not uniquely defined after
estimating variance components in an unbalanced design. Satterthwaite and
Kenward--Roger methods approximate finite-sample uncertainty in different ways;
software defaults should therefore be reported rather than hidden.

Profile-likelihood intervals can better represent asymmetric uncertainty.
Parametric bootstrap can propagate covariance estimation and nonlinearity if the
fitted data-generating model is credible and the complete fitting procedure is
repeated. None of these methods corrects pseudoreplication, informative missing
data, model selection, or an unsupported causal interpretation.

# Random Effects and Prediction

Given covariance parameters, the conditional mean of the random effects is

$$
E(\mathbf b\mid\mathbf y)
=\mathbf G\mathbf Z^\mathsf{T}\mathbf V^{-1}
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta).
$$

Plugging in estimated parameters produces empirical BLUPs. Their shrinkage is a
strength for prediction but changes their sampling behavior. A conditional
prediction interval for another observation from an existing unit differs from
a marginal interval for a new unit: the latter must include new random-effect
variation. State which population and level the prediction concerns.

Random-effect estimates can be useful for checking the model or predicting
sampled units, but naive histograms and normal Q--Q plots of heavily shrunken
BLUPs do not display the latent distribution without distortion. Likewise,
regressing an outcome on estimated BLUPs in a second stage ignores their
uncertainty and can induce bias.

# Missing and Unbalanced Data

Mixed models naturally accommodate unequal observation counts and irregular
measurement times when the likelihood and covariance model are correctly
specified. This is not the same as being immune to missingness.

Likelihood-based inference is generally justified when missingness is ignorable
under the stated model—for example, missing at random given observed outcomes
and covariates, together with distinct missingness parameters. Dropout depending
on an unobserved current outcome or latent trajectory can make standard mixed
model estimates biased. Record reasons for missingness, include relevant
observed predictors, and use sensitivity models for plausible missing-not-at-
random mechanisms.

# Model Specification and Diagnostics

A useful workflow separates design, fitting, and criticism:

1. Identify biological units, repeated measurements, crossed or nested factors,
   and the target generalization.
2. Specify a scientifically interpretable fixed-effect mean, including required
   interactions and nonlinear time terms.
3. Encode design-supported random effects and any residual correlation or
   heterogeneous variance.
4. Check rank, group counts, within-group predictor variation, scaling, and
   optimizer convergence.
5. Examine marginal and conditional residuals, unit trajectories, fitted versus
   observed patterns, influence, and predictive performance at the correct unit.
6. Repeat key conclusions across plausible mean, covariance, and missingness
   specifications.

| Warning | Possible mechanism | Useful response |
|---|---|---|
| Nonconvergence or large gradients | poor scaling, weak identification, unsuitable optimizer, overcomplex model | rescale, inspect design support, try validated optimizers, simplify transparently |
| Singular covariance estimate | zero or weakly identified component, too few informative groups | inspect within-group variation and report sensitivity |
| Residual trend or curvature | wrong mean trajectory or interaction | revise fixed effects before interpreting covariance |
| Residual spread varies | heteroskedasticity or wrong transformation | model variance by group/time or choose an outcome-appropriate model |
| Remaining serial pattern | random effects do not capture short-range residual dependence | add justified residual correlation and compare predictions |
| One group dominates | leverage, sparse treatment-by-group support, data error | verify data and perform leave-group-out influence analysis |

Gaussian random effects and residuals are distributional assumptions. Fixed-
effect estimates can sometimes be fairly robust to moderate shape deviations,
but tail probabilities, variance components, BLUPs, and predictions may not be.
Simulation from the fitted model and cluster-level resampling can reveal whether
the intended inferential procedure is calibrated for the actual group count and
imbalance.

# Worked Bioinformatics Example

Suppose 60 patients contribute tumor biopsies before treatment and at two
follow-up times. RNA abundance for a prespecified pathway score is measured from
each biopsy, sometimes in duplicate libraries. Patients are recruited at four
sites and processing batches overlap imperfectly with time.

A defensible model could include fixed effects for treatment, time, their
interaction, baseline clinical covariates, and processing batch; patient random
intercepts and time slopes; and a site effect if the sampling target and number
of sites support it. Duplicate libraries are technical measurements. They may be
summarized using measurement precision or represented by an explicit technical
level, but they do not double the patient sample size.

The treatment-by-time contrast estimates a mean difference in pathway-score
change for the modeled patient population. The patient slope variance describes
unexplained trajectory heterogeneity. A conditional fitted curve describes a
sampled patient; a prediction for a new patient includes between-patient
variation. If dropout is related to unobserved disease progression, a standard
MAR likelihood analysis needs an MNAR sensitivity analysis.

Statistically significant mean change is not necessarily biologically large or
mechanistically attributable to treatment. Report the score scale, uncertainty,
patient-level trajectories, heterogeneity, missingness, and whether the site and
batch design supports transport beyond the observed centers.

  empirical BLUPs.
- [Sensitivity analysis and robustness](../statistical-inference/sensitivity-analysis-and-robustness.qmd)
  organizes conclusions across credible alternatives.

1. A linear mixed model combines a fixed-effect mean with covariance induced by
   random effects and residual structure.
2. Population contrasts, variance components, existing-unit predictions, and
   new-unit predictions are different estimands.
3. ML and REML serve different comparison and estimation roles; boundary and
   small-group problems invalidate automatic asymptotic tests.
4. Convergence is computational evidence, not proof that the mean, covariance,
   missingness, or causal model is adequate.
5. Biological experimental units determine independent information; technical
   measurements must remain nested in that design.
